summary: This Informational document classifies design goals and security considerations for hybrid digital signature schemes. It covers proof composability, non-separability of the component signatures, backward and forward compatibility, hybrid generality, and Simultaneous Verification.

eli5.summary: A signature made with two pens at once. This describes the choices in how the two are combined and which tradeoffs each choice brings.

subtitle: Taxonomy of design choices and security tradeoffs for hybrid digital signatures.

tldr.problem: Hybrid signatures that combine post-quantum and traditional algorithms can be designed in many ways, each with different security guarantees and tradeoffs that system architects must understand.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC documents design goals such as non-separability, backwards compatibility, and simultaneous verification, and shows how different hybrid approaches achieve or fail different combinations of these goals.
tldr.outcome: No single hybrid design achieves all goals simultaneously; architects must choose which properties matter most for their use case.

today: RFC 9955 is an Informational RFC that provides guidance to designers and implementers choosing hybrid signature approaches. It does not recommend a specific design but rather documents the landscape of tradeoffs. The document helps architects understand which properties their use case requires.

sections.title: The Hybrid Signature Challenge
sections.content:
Digital signatures prove who sent a message. They are the foundation of authentication in certificates, contracts, and secure protocols. As quantum computers pose a threat, cryptographers want to transition to post-quantum signature schemes. However, post-quantum algorithms are new and less well-studied than RSA or ECDSA. A hybrid signature combines a traditional algorithm with a post-quantum one so that authentication remains valid as long as at least one algorithm is unbroken.

But designing a good hybrid signature is subtle. Simply concatenating two signatures, for example, leaves open the possibility that an attacker with a quantum computer could remove the post-quantum signature and forge a traditional-only signature. The RFC explores the design landscape: different ways to combine signatures, different security guarantees each provides, and fundamental tradeoffs where achieving one goal prevents another.
sections.eli5: If you sign something with two pens at once, you need to think carefully about how to make sure both signatures are really there and cannot be separated.

sections.title: Core Concepts and Definitions
sections.content:
A hybrid signature scheme combines two or more component signature algorithms. The document carefully defines terminology: a signature scheme has three parts (key generation, signing, and verification), a hybrid signature is the output of the combined scheme, and component schemes are the algorithms that are combined.

A critical concept is separability. If an attacker can take a hybrid signature and extract a valid traditional signature without the post-quantum part, the signature is separable and vulnerable to stripping attacks. Another key concept is proof composability: can the security of the hybrid be proven from the security of its components, or must it be analyzed from scratch?
sections.eli5: A stripping attack is when someone tears off one signature and leaves the other. A good hybrid design makes that impossible or leaves obvious evidence.

sections.title: Non-Separability Spectrum
sections.content:
The RFC defines a spectrum of non-separability from weakest to strongest. At one end, no non-separability: an attacker can simply remove the post-quantum signature and the result looks fine. Next, weak non-separability (WNS): artifacts remain if a signature is stripped, but verification might still succeed unless the system checks for artifacts. Third, strong non-separability (SNS): the hybrid signature is designed so that removing either component causes verification to fail cryptographically. Finally, SNS with simultaneous verification: both components are verified together, and no partial information about either is leaked until both are checked.

SNS is harder to achieve but stronger: an honest verifier cannot be tricked into accepting a stripped signature. Schemes using concatenation without artifacts provide no non-separability; nested or fused schemes can achieve SNS.
sections.eli5: No non-separability means a signature can be ripped apart and the pieces still work. Strong non-separability means the two signatures are tangled together so tightly that tearing them apart breaks both.

sections.title: Artifacts and Detection
sections.content:
An artifact is evidence that a signature was meant to be hybrid even if one component is removed. Artifacts can live at different levels: in the signature itself, in the certificate chain, in the protocol, or in the message. For example, a message might contain a label saying this document must be signed with both algorithms, or the signature itself might encode a hybrid identifier.

The location of artifacts matters for security analysis. If an artifact lives in the message, an attacker who forges the traditional signature can also remove the artifact. If the artifact is in the signature itself (as in fused constructions), it cannot be separated from the cryptographic result. If the artifact is in the certificate chain, the entire certificate path must support the hybrid approach.
sections.eli5: An artifact is a clue that proves two signatures were used together. The better the clue is protected, the harder it is to fake.

sections.title: Design Goals and Tradeoffs
sections.content:
The RFC enumerates ten design goals, including hybrid authentication (security via at least one component), proof composability (reduce security proofs to components), backwards compatibility (legacy verifiers can verify only one signature), simultaneous verification (both components verified together), and high performance and space efficiency. Each is desirable, but not all can be achieved together.

For example, backwards compatibility and strong non-separability are mutually exclusive: if a legacy system is allowed to verify only the traditional signature, then the post-quantum component can be stripped. Similarly, simultaneous verification and low need for approval tend to conflict: achieving simultaneous verification often requires entangling the component algorithms, which makes certification harder. Architects must prioritize: which goals matter most for their threat model and deployment?
sections.eli5: You want the signature small, fast, secure, backwards-compatible, and unbreakable all at once. But you cannot have all of them; you have to choose which ones matter most.

sections.title: Forgery and Key Reuse Attacks
sections.content:
A subtle vulnerability is the component algorithm forgery attack. If the same key pair is used for both the hybrid scheme and the traditional component alone, an attacker with a quantum computer could forge a traditional signature on the same key. The hybrid signature might have combined both properly, but the component signature is a forgery. This is especially dangerous in concatenation schemes where the two signatures are verified separately.

The document recommends restricting key reuse: forbid using the same key for both hybrid and component verification. This must be enforced through system policy and certificates, not cryptography alone. Alternatively, choose a hybrid design that provides strong non-separability, making component forgery impossible by construction.
sections.eli5: If you use the same key to sign both ways (hybrid and alone), a bad guy could fake the traditional signature. The fix is to use different keys for each, or use a design where the two signatures cannot be separated.

viz.caption: Non-separability increases from weakest (top) to strongest (bottom).

layers.label: No Non-Separability
layers.detail: Attacker can strip signatures with no artifacts left.

layers.label: Weak Non-Separability
layers.detail: Artifacts remain if stripped, but verification may succeed.

layers.label: Strong Non-Separability
layers.detail: Removal causes cryptographic verification to fail.

layers.label: SNS + Simultaneous Verification
layers.detail: Both verified together; no partial information leaked.
